11.5 Phase Equilibrium in S olutions: Nonvolatile Solutes

We turn now from the chemical reactions of solutions to such physical properties as their vapor pressures and phase diagrams. Consider first a solution made by dissolving a nonvolatile solute in a solvent. By “nonvolatile” we mean that the vapor pressure of the solute above the solution is negligible. An example is a solu- tion of sucrose (cane sugar) in water, in which the vapor pressure of sucrose above the solution is zero. We study the case of a volatile solute in Section 11.6.

The solvent vapor pressure is not zero and changes with the composition of the solution at a fixed temperature.
